prime.problem: The max of each window of k numbers costs k − 1 comparisons if you rescan: 98,901,999 for n = 10⁵, k = 10³. A heap with lazy deletion is O(n log n) and can pile up stale entries.
prime.fits: Follows the counts window: same forward-only sweep, but with a fixed width. It uses the toolkit's deque for O(1) work at both ends, and the amortized argument from the Big-O card.
expect: a deque of indices whose values never rise
back pops: new values beat older, smaller ones
front expiry: the index that slid out
why each index is pushed once and popped at most once
prime.goal: Compute every sliding-window maximum in O(n) time and O(k) memory, and explain why an element beaten from the back can never be a max again.

attend: Why is it safe to throw away a smaller value that is older than the new one?
Why does the deque store indices rather than values?
Why can at most one index expire from the front per step?
The while loop can pop many items in one step. Why is the whole pass still O(n)?
What must change to get the window minimum instead?

must: A new x arrives → every older value smaller than x will leave the window before x does and is smaller → it can never be a max again → pop it from the back → values in the deque never rise from front to back → the front is the window's max
The window slides one step → at most the front index falls out (front ≤ i − k) → store indices so expiry is a comparison → the deque only holds in-window indices → O(k) memory
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, from either end → all the while loops together run ≤ n times → at most 2n deque operations, O(n) total whatever k is
elevated: Pop only strictly smaller values (<) → equal values stay → the older equal expires first while the newer one still covers the max → either < or <= gives correct maxima, but < keeps duplicates in the deque
reference: the source's decrement of k and its front < i − k form
sparse tables as the O(1)-query, O(n log n)-build alternative
jump game VI and shortest subarray with sum ≥ K as further uses

compress.prompt: From memory, state the deque's invariant in one sentence, then write the three moves of each step (expire, beat, push) and one sentence on why the total is O(n).
checklist: invariant: in-window indices whose values never rise front to back
expire the front if it is ≤ i − k
pop from the back while its value < x, then push i
each index is pushed once and popped at most once: ≤ 2n operations

retrieve.q: Explain why the value 3 at index 1 is still in the deque at i = 3 even though −1 and −3 arrived after it.
answer: new values only pop smaller values from the back
−1 and −3 are smaller than 3, so they queue behind it
3 stays the front and the max until it expires at i = 4

retrieve.q: Walk through step i = 4 (x = 5) with the deque holding 3@1, −1@2, −3@3 and k = 3.
answer: expiry: front index 1 ≤ 4 − 3, so 3@1 leaves from the front
beat: −3 < 5 and −1 < 5 are popped from the back
push 5@4; the deque is [5@4] and the max is 5

retrieve.q: A colleague proposes a max-heap of (−x, i) with lazy deletion instead. What does it cost, and on which input does it get worst?
answer: O(n log n) instead of O(n)
stale entries leave only when they reach the top
on a strictly rising array each new value becomes the top, so old ones never surface and pile up toward n entries
the deque never holds more than k indices

compare.q: Monotonic deque vs monotonic stack: which ends does each drop from, what does the popped element learn, and when does a stack stop being enough?
answer: the stack drops only from the top; the deque also drops expired indices from the front
a stack pop means the new element is the popped one's nearest smaller or larger neighbour (its wall)
a deque back-pop means the popped one can never be a max again; the front is the answer
when elements also expire from the left (a sliding window), a stack can't remove them: use the deque

compare.q: Both handle a fixed window of k. Why can the max throw values away forever while the median can't?
answer: a smaller, older value can never become the max again, so discarding it is safe
any value can become the median as others leave, so the median needs the whole window
the median keeps all k values in two heaps with lazy deletion: O(log) per step
the max needs only the dominating subsequence: O(1) amortized

predict.q: Flip the comparison to compute the window minimum on the same nums and k = 3. Before running: what's the output, and do the pushes and pops still total at most 2n?
predict.answer: [−1, −3, −3, −3, 3, 3]. Pop from the back while the back's value is greater than x. The counts are 8 pushes and 5 pops, 13 operations, within the 2n = 16 bound, because each index still enters once and leaves at most once.

apply.task: Modify max_sliding_window into min_sliding_window and add counters for pushes and pops. Run it on [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7] with k = 3, then write the deque after each step as the card's trace does.
apply.done: Output [−1, −3, −3, −3, 3, 3] with 8 pushes and 5 pops, and your trace shows values never falling from front to back.
apply.hint: Only the comparison in the while loop changes.
